blocks.text: **Proximal humerus fractures** occur at the top of the upper arm bone, usually in older adults with osteoporosis after a fall onto an outstretched hand or directly onto the shoulder. Most are minimally displaced and treated without surgery in a sling, followed by early movement [Ref – to verify]. Displaced or complex fractures may need fixation or joint replacement.

**Clavicle fractures** are common in young adults after a fall or sport collision. Most occur in the middle third. Many are treated non-operatively; significantly displaced or shortened fractures may be fixed surgically [Ref – to verify].
The physiotherapist's tasks: confirm the medical plan and weight-bearing restrictions, start safe movement early, prevent stiffness, and rebuild strength and function.

items: Pain, swelling and bruising (often spreading down the arm after a few days in proximal humerus fractures). Inability or unwillingness to lift the arm.
Clavicle: visible deformity, tenderness over the bone.

Neurovascular screen: radial pulse, hand colour, sensation over the "regimental badge" area (lateral deltoid, axillary nerve), deltoid isometric activation.
Elbow, wrist and hand range (these stiffen quickly if ignored).
Shoulder range only within allowed limits: start with passive or active-assisted movement as permitted.
Posture, cervical and thoracic screen.

blocks.text: Special tests for soft tissue (impingement or cuff tests) are not used in the early fracture phase. Later, assess rotator cuff integrity, because cuff tears can accompany fractures in older adults.

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Cold, pale hand, weak or absent pulse
New or worsening numbness or weakness
Increasing pain and deformity during rehabilitation
Fracture after trivial force with weight loss or cancer history

steps: **Confirm fracture type, management, and allowed movement.**
**Phase 1 (protection):** sling, hand, wrist, elbow exercises, pendulum or passive movement as allowed.
**Phase 2 (when the surgeon confirms healing, often around 3 to 6 weeks):** active-assisted then active range.

rows: Glenohumeral glides (grades I to II then III to IV)
After healing confirmed with persistent stiffness
Reduces associated neck and upper back pain

rows: Hand squeezes, wrist and elbow range
Lean forward, support on a table, let the arm hang and sway in small circles by moving the body

Use a stick or slide hand on a table
Active elevation, isometric then band rotator cuff work

blocks.text: Ice for pain early; heat before stretching later. Other modalities not routinely needed.

items: Phase 1 (about 0 to 3 weeks): protect, control pain, keep the hand, elbow and neck moving, early gentle shoulder movement as allowed.
Phase 2 (about 3 to 6 weeks): restore range.
Phase 3 (from about 6 to 12 weeks): strength, function, return to activity.
Bone health referral and falls prevention for older adults.

blocks.text: Timelines vary with fracture type and surgery; follow medical guidance.
Range of motion (flexion, abduction, external rotation), pain, QuickDASH or Oxford Shoulder Score, ability to perform self-care.

items: **Why move the elbow and hand from day 1?** They stiffen quickly and are not at risk from the fracture.
**Which nerve is most at risk with proximal humerus fractures?** Axillary nerve: check deltoid and lateral arm sensation.
**Why do pendulum exercises use body sway?** To move the shoulder passively without active muscle pull across the fracture.
**An 80-year-old has a fracture after tripping. What else must be addressed?** Falls prevention and bone health.
**Pain and deformity increase at week 3. What do you do?** Stop exercises and contact the surgical team for imaging.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Perform a neurovascular check after shoulder fracture.
Plan phase-based rehabilitation within medical restrictions.
Address falls and bone health.
